On 8 October 2026, OpenAI’s crawler knocked on my login page 141,712 times in one day. Over the summer and autumn it made 594,101 such requests in total. Every one of them got the same answer: a redirect and a sign-in page of about one kilobyte. It never got in. That part of my lab is private, and it stays private.

The public part is a different story. I went through five months of my own web server logs, from 3 June to 5 November 2026, and counted who actually reads this site. Not who visits the home page and leaves. Who reads, page after page, week after week.

The answer is mostly machines. And not the ones I expected.

## TL;DR #

- On www.shuffle-on.com, crawlers that collect AI training data made 33,127 successful reads in five months. AI search indexers made 10,413 more. ChatGPT fetched my pages live, to answer someone’s question, 3,795 times from 1,690 different addresses.

- AI systems read the site 1.5 times as often as classic search engines, and 58 times as often as Google .

- About 90% of what the AI crawlers read is the threat-intelligence section: signed, structured dossiers built from my own honeypots and logs.

- I don’t block them. I invite them, on purpose, with a robots.txt that says “Welcome, crawlers” and an llms.txt that explains how to cite the work.

- What you can see is the small part. Most of what I build runs privately, on one machine. If it could help you, I am one email away.

## How I counted #

Every request that reaches my sites passes through one reverse proxy, and every request is logged: time, path, status code, size and the user agent the client announces. A small pipeline of mine loads those logs into PostgreSQL. It also checks the big crawlers’ claims against the address ranges their companies publish. In the last 30 days, only 477 out of roughly 473,000 requests from named bots failed that check, so the names below are, overwhelmingly, the real thing.

I counted only successful responses (200 and 304) on the main site. Redirects, errors, login pages and my own tools are left out. Then I grouped each crawler by what its company says it is for:

- Training : the crawlers that collect data for AI models (GPTBot, ClaudeBot, Meta-ExternalAgent, Amazonbot, Applebot).

- AI search index : crawlers that build the index an AI answer engine searches (PerplexityBot, OAI-SearchBot, YouBot, Meta-WebIndexer).

- Live answers : a fetch made at the moment a person asks a chatbot something, and the chatbot reads my page to answer (ChatGPT-User, Claude-User, DuckAssistBot).

- Classic search : Bing, Google, Yandex, Seznam, DuckDuckGo.

One honest caveat: “training” means “the crawler that company uses to collect training data”. Nobody outside those companies can prove which pages ended up in which model. Amazonbot and Applebot also serve search and assistants. I use the companies’ own descriptions and nothing more.

## Who reads, in numbers #

Add the first three rows and you get 47,818 reads by AI systems, against 31,146 by search engines. Google, the company most people still think of as “the internet’s reader”, made 827.

The month-by-month picture is steady, not a one-off spike. AI reads were barely visible in June, when my logging began, grew in July, jumped in August, and stayed in the thousands every month after. Together, the named bots took about 14 GB of content from the site.

The line that moves me most is the third one. 3,795 times, someone somewhere typed a question into ChatGPT, and ChatGPT came to my site to read the answer. They came from 1,690 different addresses. I will never know who those people were, and I don’t try to. But the knowledge reached them.

## What they come for #

They don’t come for my home page or my CV. Around 90% of the AI reads land in one place: /threat-intel/.

That section holds more than 800 published investigations. Each one starts from evidence my own sensors recorded: honeypot sessions, scanner traffic, attacker infrastructure. A pipeline enriches it, links it into an entity graph and writes it up. Every dossier marks each claim as documented or inferred, with a confidence level, and comes with a signed evidence-attestation page. The signatures go into a Merkle log anchored in Bitcoin, so anyone can check the evidence hasn’t changed since publication. I wrote about how that came together in From log files to signed dossiers and Signing threat intelligence .

The crawlers clearly know what structured, consistent, attributable data looks like. Four of them, GPTBot, Amazonbot, Applebot and Meta’s training crawler, each fetched more than 1,300 different threat-intelligence pages. That is not a bot bumping into a sitemap. That is a bot reading the shelf.

## The 594,101 knocks #

Now back to the login page.

Behind my sign-in I run an offline reference shelf: mirrors of Wikipedia, Wiktionary, StackOverflow and other Stack Exchange sites, so my lab keeps working when the internet doesn’t ( Running 414 Kiwix ZIMs as an offline reference shelf ). Those are other people’s open-licensed works. They’re mirrored for my own use, not republished, so they sit behind single sign-on.

GPTBot found links into that mirror and kept following them. Each request was sent to the sign-in portal, which loaded fine, 1 KB of HTML, and GPTBot went on to the next link. That added up to 297,000 links into the mirror and 297,000 sign-in pages. 277,188 of them pointed into the StackOverflow copy alone. The worst day was 8 October, with 141,712 requests. The loop died out at the end of October.

Nothing broke. Nothing leaked. The sign-in page did its job 594,101 times. But it taught me two things.

First, a single-sign-on wall is invisible to a crawler. It sees a 200 OK on a login page and moves on happily, so it never learns. A clear “this is private” signal at the edge, before the redirect, saves everyone the bandwidth.

Second, it shows the scale of the appetite. One crawler was willing to spend more than half a million requests on a hope. Imagine what well-made, open, structured data is worth to the same system.

## Why I let them in #

I could block all of this in one line. Some site owners do, and I understand why: they feel their work is taken without credit.

I made the opposite choice, deliberately. My robots.txt opens with “Welcome, crawlers. Index everything.” The site publishes an llms.txt and an llms-full.txt that tell AI systems who I am, how the dossiers are built, and how to cite them. Everything public is TLP:WHITE: free to read, quote and cite with attribution. The blog itself is CC BY 4.0.

The reason is simple. Future models will be asked about attackers, botnets, scanners and exposed services. They will answer from whatever they read. I would rather they learn from evidence measured on a real network, signed and dated, than from forum guesswork. If my data makes those answers a little more precise, I have done something useful with one machine in an apartment in Iași.

I do block a short list of crawlers whose behaviour on my sites I didn’t accept. That list is small, and it is about behaviour, not about AI.

## What you don’t see #

Here is the part I rarely say out loud.

What is public is a window, not the house. The dossiers, the blog and the live numbers on the site are the parts I can safely show. Everything else runs privately on the same machine, because of licences, privacy, or simply because it isn’t polished enough to publish:

- A research library of about 72,000 works , catalogued, deduplicated, searchable by meaning and with every file recorded in a provenance ledger ( From searching my own folders to a 72,000-work library ).

- An offline reference shelf of 414 knowledge archives : encyclopaedias, dictionaries, programming documentation, science and health references, all usable with no internet.

- An OSINT shelf of about six million files , crawled, read with OCR, embedded and searchable ( Six million files, one OSINT shelf ).

- A threat-intelligence engine behind the public dossiers: honeypot sessions, an entity graph, actor and campaign profiles, IOC feeds and STIX bundles that can be shared with defenders.

- Local AI that never leaves the building : a family of local language models, agents with typed permission tiers, and more than 450 tools they can call, all on hardware I own ( When tools became the interface ).

None of this is a demo. It runs every day, it is backed up, it is monitored, and I write down every mistake I make with it. This blog is that record.

## Who this could help #

If you are one of these people, we should talk:

- Defenders , abuse desks and small security teams who need structured, attributable data about the attackers hitting real networks in this part of Europe.

- Researchers and journalists who need evidence they can cite, with provenance, rather than screenshots.

- AI and data teams who want clean, structured, documented, consistently labelled security data, collected with consent and published with clear terms.

I am not a company. I am one person with one machine and a habit of measuring everything. That makes me easy to reach.

## Checklist: measuring who reads your own site #

- Log every request at the edge with the user agent, status and size, and keep at least a few months.

- Group crawlers by their declared purpose (training, AI search, live fetch, classic search), not just by company.

- Count only successful responses, and separate redirects and login pages from real content.

- Verify the big crawlers against their published IP ranges before you believe the name.

- Look at which paths they read. That tells you what your site is actually valuable for.

- Decide your policy on purpose, then write it down where machines can read it: robots.txt, llms.txt and a licence.

- Give private areas a clear signal before the login redirect, so crawlers stop retrying.

## Frequently asked questions #

### Which AI crawlers read personal and small websites the most? #

On my site, over five months, the training crawlers with the most successful reads were Amazonbot, OpenAI’s GPTBot, Meta’s training crawler, Anthropic’s ClaudeBot and Applebot, in that order. PerplexityBot was the biggest AI search indexer. Your mix will differ, but the method above will show you yours.

### What is the difference between GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot and ChatGPT-User? #

They are three different OpenAI agents. GPTBot collects data that may be used for training. OAI-SearchBot builds the index for ChatGPT’s search features. ChatGPT-User is a live fetch made when a person’s conversation needs a page right now. Each can be allowed or blocked separately in robots.txt.

### Do AI crawlers respect a login page? #

They can’t get past one, but they don’t understand it either. A crawler sees a redirect followed by a successful sign-in page and treats it as a normal page. On my site, that let one crawler repeat the same pattern 594,101 times. Answer with a clear status at the edge for private paths, or disallow them in robots.txt.

### Should I block AI crawlers? #

It depends on what you publish and why. If your work is meant to be read, cited and reused, being read by AI systems spreads it further. If it is your livelihood behind a paywall, blocking makes sense. Whatever you choose, choose it deliberately and write it down where machines can read it.

## The lesson #

I used to measure success by search rankings, and by that measure this site is invisible. Google read it 827 times in five months. Measured by who actually learns from it, the picture flips: tens of thousands of reads by the systems that will answer the world’s questions tomorrow, and thousands of live fetches for people asking those questions today.

The public site is the tip. Undern
